title: Should Child Psychiatry Become an Interventional Specialty?
subtitle: A new review by Coarkin, et. al. adds yet more data in favor of TMS in youth.
body_html:
Antidepressants in youth have a big problem—a black box warning for “increased suicidal thoughts.” This is a warning from the FDA that is so important it is, by law, included in the consent process every time these medicines are prescribed. Welcome to The Frontier Psychiatrists Newsletter. I’m Owen Scott Muir, M.D., DFAACAP and I’m a Child and Adult Psychiatrist and the Chief Medical Officer of Radial + of Neurolief.

Thinking about suicide is not as bad as death by suicide, but it’s not good. It’s both scary for the adolescent, the families, and the health professionals. It can lead to hospital admissions, which, as I’ve amply covered, can be traumatic and risky in some cohorts. Even if an adolescent tells no one that they are thinking about suicide, it sucks to walk around thinking about suicide.

It’s isolating—if I tell someone, what will happen?!?

It drains the color and joy out of life, as you struggle not to mention it while you go through the day.

It makes it hard to answer the question “hey, what are you thinking about?” from your first girlfriend or boyfriend.

But, absent other options for the treatment of depression, it is hard to know what to do. It would be wonderful if there were a treatment option for depression that had large-scale data to relieve depression, which also didn’t make things worse.

An Advertising Moment:

At Radial—where I work—we have experience with non-medication treatment for adolescent depression. This includes TMS, dTMS, PRISM, and SAINT fMRI-guided accelerated TMS.

Radial offers the most advanced mental health care. Our doctors have treated more adolescents with brain stimulation than almost anyone else.

Get Care At Radial

And, today, thanks to Paul Coarkin, DO, MS, and colleagues in JAACAP Open1, we have the largest scale review to date of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in n=682 adolescents (age 12-19) and another n=601 young adults (age 20-21). This is data from the “TrakStar” data base, which is maintained by Neuronetics to follow those treated with their figure-8 coil systems.

The Effectiveness of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Adolescents and Young Adults With Major Depressive Disorder

The very short version: TMS works well in adolescent depression!

In youth who get too few treatments, it’s less effective. In youth who get greater than 41 sessions, which is a lot more than the traditional course of 36, they may represent difficult-to-treat cohort who get benefit in terms of response rate, but with lower remission rates than their peers who require less stimulation sessions.

Most importantly, in comparison with oral medicines, the rate of cases where depression got better was high, and the rate where it got worse was low.

More than 70% of the entire sample experienced a Positive Meaningful Change, while less than 1% experienced a Negative Meaningful Change. Thus, clinically meaningful worsening of depressive symptoms was rare.1

Those “meaningful change” numbers ate >6 or <6 points on the PHQ9, which is a big difference on that scale that only goes up to 27.

It’s worth mentioning that this data isn’t out of left field. For those following my published academic work closely, which, as far as I can tell is a sample of n=2 (Me, and My Mom), these data will come as no surprise. In an open label data set from 2020, in Brain Stimulation, using BrainsWay H-coils in youth 10-21, n=12 kiddos had significant improvement:

The performance of a paired T-test demonstrated an overall signifcant reduction in baseline PHQ9 scores after a course of treatment… P < .05, d=0.55. Patients age was not correlated with reduction in PHQ9 scores (r= .01, ns.)2

And replicated in a much larger data (n=1497) set with my colleagues, with Roth, Ph.D., as lead author in 2025:

For the primary patient-rated assessment (PHQ-9), the response rates for these adolescents and young adults with treatment-resistant depression were 64.4 % (30 sessions) and 74.6 % (36 sessions). The remission rates were 25.5 % (30 sessions) and 34.6 % (36 sessions).

One seizure (0.08 %) was reported, and no other serious adverse events were reported. Other reported adverse events were all commonly seen with TMS and included headache (0.32 %), slight headache (0.08 %), tooth pain (0.16 %), fatigue (0.24 %) and left side mouth pain (0.08 %).3

The most serious adverse event (“one seizure”) was in my patient! It’s worth noting that the patient chose to continue TMS after that event with a modified protocol and extensive informed consent.

Additionally, I co-authored the following abstract published in Biological Psychiatry in 2025, on the utility of SAINT TMS in youth. SAINT is an accelerated and fMRI-guided version of this treatment, and our results were promising in light of the above larger-scale data, but in just 5 days of treatment!

Thirteen participants, aged 18-21 years (4 male, 9 female), completed treatment. Participants had a mean(SD) MADRS score of 19.9(6.1) at baseline indicating moderate depression. Following treatment, 69.2% of participants met criteria for remission (MADRS ≤10 or CGI-I ≤2 within 1 week following treatment).4

TMS—it works in adolescents. The rates of adverse effects are low, and the above non-overlapping samples represent well over 3000 published cases treated.

It’s worth noting that the FDA black box warning was based on only 4400 patients worth of data:

A total of 24 trials involving over 4400 patients were included. The analysis showed a greater risk of suicidality during the first few months of treatment in those receiving antidepressants. The average risk of such events on drug was 4%, twice the placebo risk of 2%. No suicides occurred in these trials.

And they went on to highlight:

Pediatric patients being treated with antidepressants for any indication should be closely observed for clinical worsening, as well as agitation, irritability, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior, especially during the initial few months of a course of drug therapy, or at times of dose changes, either increases or decreases. This monitoring should include daily observation by families and caregivers and frequent contact with the physician. It is also recommended that prescriptions for antidepressants be written for the smallest quantity of tablets consistent with good patient management, in order to reduce the risk of overdose.

We began this article with a paper on TMS first authored by Paul Croarkin, DO, MS, and thus its only fitting we let him have the last word, this time from a paper he senior authored on the adverse effects of oral antidepressants in youth:

The relative severity/burden of total physical symptoms (p < 0.001), insomnia (p = 0.001), restlessness (p < 0.001), nausea (p = 0.002), abdominal pain (p < 0.001), and dry mouth (p = 0.024) decreased from baseline over 12  weeks of sertraline treatment, raising the possibility that these symptoms are transient. No significant changes were observed for sweating (p = 0.103), constipation (p = 0.241), or diarrhea (p = 0.489). Finally, we review the antidepressant withdrawal syndrome in children and adolescents and provide guidance for SSRI discontinuation, using pediatric pharmacokinetic models of escitalopram and sertraline—two of the most used SSRIs in youth.5

Those side effects are worse, in the beginning and the medicines may be harder to discontinue later.

Dear Child Psychiatrists…

It is time to review the data, and consider carefully the treatments we are offering to minimize the risks and improve the likelihood of remission from depression.
